items.title: A datetime library for Rust
items.content:
Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the

pit of success . Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to

daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the

API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”

This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience : Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

Locale Sensitive Formatting via ICU4X Integration

Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd,

Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal

implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit

to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff

to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other

libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means

semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the

ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please

In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the

intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of

time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time . A human’s concept

of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian

calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every

datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime

handling has historically been very difficult . My own belief is

that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain . Instead of

encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime

libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead

tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to

do something wrong. ( Jiff is not the first to do this! )

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project

Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code

and replace whatever is in src/main.rs . Then run the program:

I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered

with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a

shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms,

like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through

exploration in the sections that follow.)

Civil time : The time you see on your clock. And in general, the time that

the humans in your approximate geographic vicinity also see. That is, civil

time is a human coordinated agreement for communicating time in a particular

geographic region. Civil time is also known as: local time, plain time, naive

UTC : An abbreviation for Coordinated Universal Time ; it is a time

standard that serves as the basis for civil time around the world. It was

originally intended to roughly correspond to mean solar time .

TAI : An abbreviation for International Atomic Time ; it is a time standard

as measured by atomic clocks. It isn’t directly connected to mean solar time.

Leap second : An adjustment to TAI to bring it closer to mean solar time

Unix time : UTC, but ignoring leap seconds.

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here

in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

items.title: The Chinese spy allegation that toppled Nvidia's CEO is starting to look shaky
items.content:
I'm not a conspiracy theorist. But sometimes new information emerges that makes a wild theory worth considering.

That's where I find myself with the extraordinary downfall of Jensen Huang , the cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia , America's most important AI company.

Huang resigned this week after revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing.

The woman, Alice Huang , was also an executive at a company that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's powerful AI chips and has been investigated over concerns that some of those products may have been illegally diverted to China .

The allegations were explosive. Nvidia's board moved surprisingly quickly; Huang was out, and the company's stock plunged, wiping about $300 billion off its market value.

But now some of America's most respected news organizations are publishing well-sourced reports that raise serious questions about the central allegation in this scandal.

And those reports point toward another possible explanation for Huang's abrupt departure. What if the spy allegations were exaggerated to achieve a political goal?

That might sound like a conspiracy theory. Until a few days ago, I would have been reluctant to give it much consideration. Now I'm not so sure.

On Thursday, CNN reported that US intelligence agencies have not established that Alice Huang was actually spying for China.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

There is disagreement among officials about whether she was recruited by China's intelligence services. Some CIA officials are unconvinced that intercepted communications prove she knowingly passed information to Beijing.

The lead reporter on this explosive piece is Natasha Bertrand , an accomplished national security reporter whose investigations have scrutinized both Republican and Democratic administrations, and whose reporting on Russia's invasion of Ukraine helped earn her team an Emmy.

The possibility that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence agent was likely the key reason Nvidia's board ousted Jensen Huang so quickly. (Business Insider has not confirmed whether Alice Huang was or is a Chinese spy.)

Now, there's an open letter calling for the board to reinstate him as CEO until this is cleared up. It has over 100,000 signatures, including top executives and current Nvidia employees.

"We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy," the letter reads. "Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen's leadership."

On Friday, The Washington Post reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a prominent China hawk, took a less conclusive CIA intelligence report and used it to write his own memo warning President Donald Trump about Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

According to a person familiar with the matter, Rubio recast the CIA's findings in more assertive language. The memo's findings eventually leaked, setting off the chain of events that ended Huang's 33-year reign at Nvidia, according to the Washington Post.

"The alleged source claiming that Secretary Rubio recast a CIA report on this or for that matter any topic is a fraud who is lying to promote their own agenda," a State Department official told Business Insider. "Reporting like this is why no one takes the Washington Post seriously anymore."

The Post's reporting doesn't prove Rubio deliberately misrepresented the intelligence or set out to remove Huang. But it raises a question I think deserves serious attention: Was intelligence about a possible Chinese spy amplified to help remove a powerful obstacle to tougher restrictions on China?

There's an uncomfortable historical precedent here.

items.title: Google Wallet now lets Gemini analyze your spending and suggest ways to save
items.content:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Keeping track of where your money goes every month isn’t always easy, especially when you’re juggling multiple bank accounts, credit cards, and subscriptions. Google now wants Gemini to help you make sense of your spending without sifting through all those transactions yourself.

As we first reported back in September , Google is now bringing Wallet integration to Gemini’s Personal Intelligence feature. For context, Personal Intelligence already connects Gemini to services like Gmail, YouTube , and Photos to provide more personalized answers. With Wallet joining that list, Gemini can now help you understand your spending habits and manage your budget.

To get started, you can link your bank accounts and credit cards to Google Wallet through Plaid. Once connected, open the Gemini app and mention @Google Wallet to ask questions about your finances.

The interesting part is that you wouldn’t have to manually go through your transactions to figure all this out. You could ask Gemini a question and get an answer based on your spending history. The feature is now rolling out to Gemini users in the US across the web, Android, and iOS.

However, privacy is also a concern. Google says Gemini can only read your financial information and cannot transfer, manage, or invest your money. The integration is optional, and you can disconnect your accounts at any time.

While I can see why having an AI assistant help with budgeting might appeal to some people, I’m personally not comfortable giving Gemini access to my financial information. After all, there’s a big difference between letting AI help you write an email and allowing it to see where every dollar goes. Even with Google’s safeguards, I’d be cautious about connecting my accounts. And if you do decide to try it, double-check Gemini’s suggestions before making any financial decisions.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임받을 이용자가 [매니저 위임 신청] 버튼으로 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 활동 중인 부매니저가 있으면 부매니저만, 부매니저가 없거나 모두 부재중이면 회원이 신청할 수 있습니다.

신청하면 갤러리 공지로 신청 글이 등록되고, 신청일로부터 7일간 찬성 댓글을 받은 뒤 운영자가 검토해 위임합니다. 첫 번째 위임 신청자가 신청한 날로부터 7일간 3명까지 동시 신청이 가능합니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 2개, 댓글 4개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 1일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-99311 📢 Source: Linux 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: udf: fix return value for non-recorded-allocated extents in udf_map_block() When someone creates a corrupted UDF filesystem where symlink contains other extent type than EXT_RECORDED_ALLOCATED, it can leads to a crash like: Oops: general protection fault KASAN: maybe wild-memory-access RIP: 0010:page_get_link (fs/namei.c:6503) Call Trace: vfs_readlink (fs/namei.c:6419) do_readlinkat (fs/stat.c:583) __x64_sys_readlink (fs/stat.c:605 fs/stat.c:602 fs/stat.c:602) This is because in this case udf_map_block() fails to convert return value of inode_bmap() from 1 to 0. Returned '1' propagates through udf_bread() all the way up to __page_get_link() where it ends up being treated as a folio pointer with obvious results. Move the reset to 0 line outside the if, so udf_map_block() returns either 0 or -errno, even if the extent type is not EXT_RECORDED_ALLOCATED. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-16T09:59:33.978Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-99311
items.title_ko: Linux 커널 UDF 취약점 CVE-2026-99311: 비정상 extent 처리 시 반환값 오류로 크래시 유발
items.summary_ko: Linux 커널의 udf_map_block() 함수는 EXT_RECORDED_ALLOCATED가 아닌 extent 타입을 처리할 때 inode_bmap()의 반환값 1을 0으로 바꾸지 않았다. 손상된 UDF 파일시스템의 심볼릭 링크에서 이 문제가 발생하면 잘못된 값이 folio 포인터로 취급되어 General Protection Fault와 KASAN 오류로 커널이 충돌할 수 있다. 수정안은 반환값 재설정을 조건문 밖으로 옮겨 0 또는 -errno만 반환하도록 하는 것이다.
items.content_ko: Linux 커널 UDF 파일시스템 코드에서 해결된 취약점에 대한 설명이다. udf_map_block()에서 EXT_RECORDED_ALLOCATED가 아닌 다른 extent 타입이 있을 때 inode_bmap()의 반환값 1이 0으로 바뀌지 않는다. 이 값은 udf_bread()를 거쳐 __page_get_link()까지 전달되고, 그 결과 folio 포인터로 잘못 해석되어 일반 보호 오류(General protection fault)와 KASAN 메모리 접근 경고가 나타나며 readlink 호출 과정에서 커널이 충돌한다. 손상된 UDF 구조의 파일시스템에서 심볼릭 링크가 포함된 경우가 해당된다. 수정 방법은 반환값을 0으로 재설정하는 줄을 if 조건문 밖으로 옮겨, udf_map_block()이 extent 타입과 관계없이 0 또는 -errno를 반환하도록 하는 것이다. 원문에는 CVSS 점수 0.0(NA), 원격 악용 가능성 False로 표시되어 있다.

items.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
items.content:
IT-Panne Schuld für Chlorgasunfall im Phantasialand | WDR aktuell

Wegen der Microsoft-Störung am Freitag bekam das Phantasialand nicht mit, dass zu viel Chlor im Pool war. 15 Gäste wurden verletzt.

Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook.

Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt.

Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte.

Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15.

Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus.

Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht.

Verletzungen durch Chlorgas im Phantasialand

Birgit Reckersdrees, Direktion Marketing und Sales Phantasialand

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows
items.content:
Prof Debi Fry said the Childlight findings showing reports had risen to more than 400,000 in 2025, revealed the ‘shocking’ level of child sexual exploitation. Photograph: Childlight/PA

Prof Debi Fry said the Childlight findings showing reports had risen to more than 400,000 in 2025, revealed the ‘shocking’ level of child sexual exploitation. Photograph: Childlight/PA

Reports of AI-related child sexual abuse material rise 8,400% in two years, data shows

Calls for governments to recognise sexual exploitation of children as preventable public health emergency

Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found.

A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.

The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images.

The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children .

Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation.

The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe.

Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online.

“But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.”

A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online , with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.

IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.

The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF.

Amount of AI-generated child sexual abuse material found online surged in 2025

Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year.

It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting.

Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”.

The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada.

Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.

“While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”

items.title: Why Am I So Tired If AI Is Doing All the Work?
items.content:
There’s this concept in Computer Science called thrashing . The tl;dr is that thrashing can happen when programs running on a computer are actively using more memory than can fit in RAM. The OS will keep moving data between memory and disk, making room for something by removing something else (that it will need again shortly). And, at some point, so much time goes into moving things around that the programs barely make any real progress.

Boy, oh boy, isn’t that every single one of us right now using AI? One agent is working, and you, almost by reflex, will start something else. Kind of like doomscrolling: you don’t even realize you’re doing it.

And by the way, of course we’re doing it! These apps (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) make it so easy to keep several things going at once. It feels silly to be sitting there watching the agent build your thing while you’re just passively watching.

But I think this exact behavior is what’s making a lot of us feel exhausted at the end of the day. Mostly because of that last part: multitasking.

Because when the agent comes back, you need to understand what it did before you can do anything useful with it . You open the diff 2 hours later and try to remember what you asked for… and right when you’re starting to make sense of it, another agent (with something completely different) now wants your attention 🤡

So you go there because it’s just a quick question (you think). But answering it requires remembering what that other agent was doing and why you chose that approach, etc. By the time you come back to the first one, you have to restart the whole process again.

You can spend a surprising amount of your day doing this! Even when the agents are doing a great job, you still need to get enough of each problem back into your head to know whether their output is making any sense…

I think we’re making this worse by saying yes to things we would’ve simply put on our priority queue (or just left alone) before. Because “I’ll just ask my agent” feels like such a small commitment — and easier than creating a ticket, right? — that we forget we’re also volunteering to understand, check, and finish whatever comes back .

(Btw, this reminds me of the Jevons paradox where using a resource more efficiently can lead to consuming more of it overall. Jevons was talking about coal, but I think there’s some similarity here where each task gets cheaper, so we take on more of them)

Don’t get me wrong, I still pretty much want to use AI, but I do think we need a better/more sustainable way. One OS approach when it comes to thrashing is to suspend some processes, so the others have enough memory to make progress. And maybe that’s what we should be doing as well?

I think that, at the end of the day, we might need to get comfortable with just letting an agent sit there with nothing else to do sometimes. Finish the task, make sure it works, and only then move to the next thing.

We don’t need to keep 10 agents busy all day every day just because we can; that feels like productivity but can leave us spending the whole day trying to catch up with work we asked for ourselves. And honestly, I’d like some of the time AI saves me to actually feel like time I got back.

items.title: 사생활침해, 개인정보보호법 위반, 명예훼손, 사이버불링 정황 공론화
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in client_has_state+0x10a/0x140 fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c:3718 client_has_openowners() nfsd4_exchange_id nfsd4_proc_compound nfsd_dispatch svc_process Take clp->cl_lock while client_has_openowners() walks the openowner list. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-16T09:59:33.310Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-99310
items.title_ko: Linux 커널 nfsd 취약점 CVE-2026-99310: client_has_openowners()의 cl_lock 누락으로 인한 use-after-free
items.summary_ko: Linux 커널 nfsd의 client_has_openowners()가 cl_lock 없이 openowner 목록을 순회하고 있었다. 이 때문에 자격 증명이 맞지 않는 EXCHANGE_ID 요청이 동시에 들어오면 이미 해제된 nfs4_openowner를 참조하는 use-after-free가 발생할 수 있다. 수정은 목록을 순회하는 동안 clp->cl_lock을 잡도록 하는 것이다.
items.content_ko: 이 항목은 Linux 커널 NFS 서버(nfsd)의 취약점에 대한 설명이다. client_has_openowners()는 clp->cl_openowners 목록을 순회하며 so_stateids를 읽는데, 이때 clp->cl_lock을 잡지 않는다. 한편 nfs4_put_stateowner()는 cl_lock 아래에서 openowner를 해시 목록에서 제거한 뒤 해제한다. 이 두 작업이 동시에 진행되면, 자격 증명이 맞지 않는 EXCHANGE_ID 요청으로 이미 해제된 nfs4_openowner에 접근하는 use-after-free가 발생할 수 있다. 원문에는 KASAN이 nfs4state.c의 client_has_state에서 slab-use-after-free를 보고한 호출 스택이 포함되어 있다. 수정은 client_has_openowners()가 openowner 목록을 순회하는 동안 clp->cl_lock을 획득하는 것이다.

items.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
items.content:
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI -generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute , which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI . Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI -generated images to be tagged as Public Domain .

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI -generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

items.content_ko: 필자는 AI가 생성한 코드가 모두 오픈소스여야 한다는 의견이다. 첫째, AI 모델은 RMS가 GNU 프로젝트와 자유 소프트웨어 운동을 발표한 이후 작성된 방대한 오픈소스 코드를 허락이나 적절한 출처 표기 없이 인터넷에서 수집해 학습했다. Stack Overflow와 Stack Exchange 자매 사이트 콘텐츠도 출처 표기를 법적으로 요구하는 Creative Commons 라이선스로 공개되어 있는데, 이를 독점 코드로 바꾸는 것은 라이선스 세탁처럼 느껴진다는 것이다. 둘째, 순수하게 AI가 생성한 코드는 인간이 쓴 것이 아니므로 저작권 보호를 받아서는 안 된다는 주장이다. 필자는 미국의 ‘Monkey Selfie’ 분쟁을 근거로 들며, 이 판례가 비인간은 저작권을 가질 수 없다는 원칙을 세웠고 미국 저작권청도 AI 관련 판단에서 이를 인용했다고 설명한다. Wikimedia Commons가 순수 AI 생성 이미지에 퍼블릭 도메인 태그를 요구하는 것도 같은 논리다. 다만 나라마다 저작권법이 다르며, 영국은 제한적인 저작권을 인정한다는 내용이 이어지지만 입력 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Take back your RAM.
items.content:
Billions of gigabytes. Sitting idle. In bedrooms.

In the autumn of 2026 a tech CEO went on a podcast and said it was quite terrible that ordinary people keep all that RAM in their own computers. The internet laughed, then cried. RAM Altman takes him at his word.

Zip up that hoodie, sling a RAM-hungry sack over your shoulder, and good hunting. Creep through a sleeping suburb, pull sticks out of gaming rigs, talk half-asleep residents into forty pages of Terms of Service, and hit the quarter's target before the board starts exploring options.

▶ Play it above, free, right in your browser. Desktop and phone.

Getting from house to house is half the trouble. The garden gnomes take it personally, and the traffic stops for nobody.

He joined in an advisory capacity. Nobody invited him. He drifts into whichever house you're robbing, arms swinging, and starts making it simpler. He says aluminium with all five syllables. "We removed everything that wasn't essential. Including the cup handle."

Open anything with RAM in it and the game cuts to a pixel-art close-up. Seventeen of them, from gaming rigs to smart fridges, and every mistake shows up on the noise bar.

Keyboard: WASD to walk · Shift (hold) or C (toggle) to sneak · Space to act · F to use an item · T for FLIR · Esc to pause

Phone: drag the left half of the screen to walk, or tap a spot · SNEAK, ACT, USE and FLIR buttons · pinch to zoom

There's a world leaderboard. Your score is your gigabytes times the share price, which is how the board sees you anyway.

items.title: AI-First Workflows: Code as a Strategic Weapon
items.content:
AI-First Workflows: Code as a Strategic Weapon

Why knowing how to program well is as important as ever.

When my research team published our paper on how AI outcomes correlate with code quality, we started the paper with a pun. The title of the paper was Code for Machines, Not Just Humans: Quantifying AI-Friendliness with Code Health Metrics .

That title was a play on a classic proverb from SICP that “programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute”.

That maxim is the most obvious first victim of the agentic coding revolution. Code is no longer primarily for human consumption. Rather, the code we create today will be read by machines. It’s now the other way around.

However, there’s also a risk that we throw out the baby with the agentic bathwater. Code still has an important role to play as a medium bridging human intent with agentic execution. As developers we have a clear value-add here: we can — and should — design systems that remain humanly inspectable and understandable. Prompts and specs aren’t enough for that purpose.

Natural language is the wrong abstraction level

Back in May 2026, I took a look at Spec-Driven Development (SDD) . I made the remark that SDD stands out as a revival of the belief that code is a mere artifact.

That’s a sentiment that you can literally smell in each leadership conversation around software development. Code is somehow a “solved problem”. An ancient relic, doomed to be forgotten just like the lamplighters of the 19th century.

But what if code isn’t a problem but rather a solution? Something that should complement our natural language prose?

In a recent blog post , Dave Farley made a beautiful observation:

Spec-driven development got the diagnosis right and the medium wrong

In my own agentic workflows, code plays an important role. Not as an implementation medium — that I have largely delegated to agents — but rather as a mechanism for communicating with the machines.

Designing agent-first workflows with code worth reading

Code is the perfect mechanism for instructing machines. It adds the precision needed to resolve any ambiguity. That makes executable code an excellent addition on top of any natural language spec.

Further, code also has the advantage of being compact. Granted, compactness is not a given for all programming languages (VisualBasic — I’m looking at you). But if we choose wisely, then source code can be extremely compact . This compactness is a big advantage when re-reading iterations of our spec. The key is to use code to describe the observable behavior of the feature or change we’re iterating on.

My agentic flow starts with describing the purpose and motivation for the desired change or feature. This is also the step where I specify any constraints that I’m aware of (For example: “the existing API endpoint must remain stable, so create a new endpoint for this feature”).

With the plan narrowed down, I turn to the code and capture the expected outcome as higher-level end-to-end (e2e) tests that prove the code’s behavior at the system level:

A schematic view of my agent-first workflow where tests drive the details and specifies outcomes.

Those tests are as much part of the plan as the natural language spec I started out with. And I stay in the loop to drive those e2e tests myself because those tests aren’t merely verification artifacts. Rather, they are a design and specification tool:

Define the main scenario : It’s much easier to iterate in the small, so I typically just start with one or two test scenarios.

Make the tests inspectable : I spend a disproportionate amount of time making those tests inspectable. That involves defining the domain language, building the first custom assertions, as well as a domain-specific language when the problem calls for it. (For hands-on advice on these techniques, see the guide to writing inspectable tests . )

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-99309 📢 Source: Linux 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix overflow in dacloffset bounds check
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-99309 📢 Source: Linux 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix overflow in dacloffset bounds check in build_sec_desc() When the large dacl_offset is provided, dacl_offset + sizeof(struct smb_acl) overflows on 32-bit builds and the check is passed, Which makes le16_to_cpu(ppdacl_ptr->size) read out-of-bounds. This only happens for dacl_offset in range [0xFFFFFFF8, 0xFFFFFFFF]. So the oob read is max 8 bytes preceding the allocated ppntsd. unsigned int dacl_offset = le32_to_cpu(ppntsd->dacloffset); int ppdacl_size, ntacl_size = ppntsd_size - dacl_offset; if (!dacl_offset || (dacl_offset + sizeof(struct smb_acl) > ppntsd_size)) goto out; Commit beff0bc9d69b ("ksmbd: fix overflow in dacloffset bounds check") fixes similar checks in other functions. But leaves this one out, because it is only valid for 32-bit builds. Reproduced on 32-bit ARM with KASAN, by a client sending SMB2 SET_INFO(SEC) with dacloffset=0xfffffff8, then QUERY_INFO(SEC) on the same file: BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in build_sec_desc (fs/smb/server/smbacl.c:1105) Read of size 2 at addr c2a273fa by task kworker/1:1/35 CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 35 Comm: kworker/1:1 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc2+ #5 Workqueue: ksmbd-io handle_ksmbd_work Call trace: kasan_check_range from build_sec_desc (fs/smb/server/smbacl.c:1105) build_sec_desc from smb2_query_info (fs/smb/server/smb2pdu.c:7676) smb2_query_info from handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:160) handle_ksmbd_work from process_one_work (kernel/workqueue.c:3401) process_one_work from worker_thread (kernel/workqueue.c:3473) worker_thread from kthread (kernel/kthread.c:436) Add overflow check. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-16T09:59:32.633Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-99309
items.title_ko: Linux 커널 ksmbd 취약점 CVE-2026-99309: build_sec_desc()의 dacloffset 경계 검사 오버플로
items.summary_ko: 32비트 빌드에서 dacl_offset + sizeof(struct smb_acl) 계산이 오버플로되어 경계 검사가 잘못 통과될 수 있다. 이 경우 ppdacl_ptr->size를 읽을 때 할당 범위 밖을 읽는 out-of-bounds 읽기가 발생하며, 할당된 ppntsd 앞쪽 최대 8바이트 영역이 대상이 된다. 이 조건은 dacl_offset이 0xFFFFFFF8~0xFFFFFFFF 범위일 때만 발생하며, 32비트 ARM에서 KASAN으로 재현되었다.
items.content_ko: Linux 커널 ksmbd(SMB 서버)의 build_sec_desc() 함수에서 dacl_offset 경계 검사에 오버플로 문제가 있다는 내용이다. dacl_offset과 sizeof(struct smb_acl)을 더할 때 32비트 빌드에서 값이 넘쳐 검사가 잘못 통과된다. 그 결과 le16_to_cpu(ppdacl_ptr->size)가 할당 범위 밖을 읽는다. 이 문제는 dacl_offset 값이 0xFFFFFFF8에서 0xFFFFFFFF 사이일 때만 발생하며, 읽기 범위는 할당된 ppntsd 앞쪽 최대 8바이트다. 원문에 따르면 32비트 ARM에서 KASAN으로 재현되었다. 앞서 커밋 beff0bc9d69b(‘ksmbd: fix overflow in dacloffset bounds check’)가 다른 함수들의 유사한 검사를 고쳤지만, 이 함수는 32비트 빌드에서만 유효한 문제라 그 수정에서 빠졌다고 설명한다.

items.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
items.content:
Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html . That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it

Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it

Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch . From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension://<extension UUID>/web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

const origOpen = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open ;

XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open = function ( m , url , ... a ) {

const e = /^moz-extension:\/\/[^/]+/ . exec ( url );

return origOpen . call ( this , m , url , ... a );

Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule.

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html` .

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message 1 to enable the create button and set opt .

Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image ), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image . But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script. 2

items.title: Memory management in 40 major C projects, a survey
items.content:
Memory management in 40 major C projects, a survey

A survey of 40 major C projects tracked by The Consensus shows only 8 projects allocate solely with malloc/free, only 2 projects allocate without ever using malloc/free, 15 projects make use of regions at some point, 7 projects primarily use regions to allocate, 5 primarily use garbage collection to allocate, and 3 primarily use reference counting to allocate. C Programming Languages Web Servers Compression Databases Developer Tools Operating Systems Version Control Sandboxes Machine Learning Vector Databases Apache HTTP Server Brotli Citus Emacs Erlang FreeRTOS Git HAProxy Julia LZ4 Linux Lua Neovim OCaml PHP Perl PostGIS PostgreSQL Python QEMU Redis Ruby SQLite TimescaleDB Universal Ctags Vim XZ Utils Xen Zstandard curl dqlite libdeflate llama.cpp nginx pgBouncer pgvector seL4 tmux tree-sitter zlib

Phil Eaton Artwork by Andrea Chersia Focus

You are getting early access to this article as a subscriber. Your support makes articles like this possible. Thank you. C is well known for requiring manual memory management with malloc and free. And while many major projects do actually manage memory like this, many projects also implement higher-level memory management primitives such as regions (where objects allocated within a region need not be manually freed, freeing a region frees all objects allocated within the region at once), reference counting (manually incrementing and decrementing outstanding references, freeing an object only when its references go to zero), scope-based cleanup using compiler extensions, and a number of major C projects even actually implement garbage collection (fully automatic memory management). Programmers sometimes assume that projects famous for diligence lean away from purely manual memory management. But SQLite , famous for correctness, allocates 100% manually while cURL and Redis allocate mostly manually (94% and 79%), reference counting only some of their objects. Another surprising finding is that Linux and QEMU in the last few years have been starting to use scope cleanup rules (i.e. compiler extensions) to automatically clean up memory, such as Linux's __free(kfree) and QEMU's g_autofree . The Consensus tracks and indexes code for over 400 major software infrastructure projects . This article surveys 40 of the C projects within this group, excluding test code, third-party code, and examples. Majority allocation strategy #

To discover majority allocation we count allocation call sites (which is certainly a limited metric, not accounting for sub-region or size of allocation, etc.). seL4 is an exception to much of this article since it has no heap at all. 8 projects solely allocate with malloc, implementing no other general higher-level strategy for allocating. These projects are: brotli , FreeRTOS , HAProxy , libdeflate , lz4 , SQLite , xz-utils , and zlib . 16 projects primarily, but not exclusively, allocate with malloc. 7 projects primarily, if not all exclusively, allocate with a region system. With region based allocators, objects are allocated within a region. Freeing the region frees all objects within the region. Sometiems regions can be nested. And sometimes you might still manually free an object allocated within a region. items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Italy fines Meta $880 million over accessing users' photos
items.content:
Italian regulators fined Facebook parent company Meta $880 million for accessing users' photos without their "specific" consent, the country's data protection authority said on Saturday.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them," the authority said in a statement.

Saturday's latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant. In 2021, Amazon received a more than 1.1 billion euro, or about $1.2 billion, fine for breaching competition law.

That sum was subsequently reduced to 752 million euros, or about $829 million, on appeal.

Meta may also appeal the latest fine. The tech company had not responded to a request for comment by Saturday afternoon.

Meta has been fined or ordered to pay settlements over privacy issues. items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-99308 📢 Source: Linux 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: usb: xhci: Fix bounce buffer overflow High-speed devices with out of spec 1024 byte bulk endpoints exist and are allowed by USB core, but xhci-hcd always sets packet size to 512. The exact nature of these devices isn't documented, commit fb5ee84ea72c ("USB: Accept bulk endpoints with 1024-byte maxpacket") only states that they "don't work with xHCI host controllers", whatever it means. But somebody (or a malicious device) can try, and then the driver will allocate a 512 byte bounce buffer for this endpoint and may write up to 1024 bytes into it if particular scatter-gather URBs are used, because xhci_align_td() obtains packet size from the descriptor. Fix this. As a side effect, TRBs will be aligned to the packet size chosen by the driver on all endpoints of all speeds. Alignment serves the xHC, not device, so this is fine. Only out of spec devices are affected anyway. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-16T09:59:31.923Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-99308
items.title_ko: Linux 커널 xHCI 취약점 CVE-2026-99308: 바운스 버퍼 오버플로
items.summary_ko: xhci-hcd 드라이버는 엔드포인트 패킷 크기를 항상 512바이트로 설정하지만, USB 코어는 고속 장치의 1024바이트 벌크 엔드포인트를 허용한다. 이 조합에서는 512바이트 바운스 버퍼에 최대 1024바이트가 기록될 수 있어 버퍼 오버플로가 발생한다. 수정안은 모든 속도의 모든 엔드포인트에서 TRB를 드라이버가 선택한 패킷 크기에 맞춰 정렬하도록 하는 것이다. 이 문제는 사양을 벗어난 장치에만 해당한다.
items.content_ko: Linux 커널 xHCI 드라이버(xhci-hcd)의 바운스 버퍼 오버플로 문제다. 일부 고속 장치는 사양을 벗어난 1024바이트 벌크 엔드포인트를 가지고 있으며 USB 코어도 이를 허용하지만, xhci-hcd는 패킷 크기를 항상 512로 설정한다. 그 결과 드라이버는 이 엔드포인트에 512바이트 바운스 버퍼를 할당하는데, 특정 scatter-gather URB를 사용하면 최대 1024바이트가 기록될 수 있다. xhci_align_td()가 디스크립터에서 패킷 크기를 가져오기 때문이다. 수정은 모든 속도의 모든 엔드포인트에서 TRB를 드라이버가 선택한 패킷 크기에 맞춰 정렬하도록 하는 것이다. 정렬은 장치가 아니라 xHC를 위한 것이므로 이 변경은 문제가 없다고 설명한다. 사양을 벗어난 장치에만 영향이 있다. 커밋 fb5ee84ea72c(‘USB: Accept bulk endpoints with 1024-byte maxpacket’)는 이런 엔드포인트가 xHCI 호스트 컨트롤러에서 동작하지 않는다고만 언급한다. 원문에는 CVSS 점수 0.0(NA), 원격 악용 가능성 False로 표시되어 있다.

items.title: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy
items.content:
Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy

PMTiles is a tile format which works via HTTP Range requests and can be deployed as a single file to a storage bucket.

I came across Protomaps in research for my latest project, Mapboard . 1 For most non-commercial projects, commercial APIs become prohibitively expensive if you ever go viral (Mapbox, for instance, charges $5 per 1k map loads once you’ve exhausted the free tier).

PMTiles, part of the Protomaps ecosystem, is a tile format that ships in a single file, accessible via Range requests, and is thus extremely portable and easy to deploy. For CDNs that support caching Range requests of large files, it requires no effort besides down- and uploading it to storage. For others, like Cloudflare, you can utilize an edge function to translate between the traditional x/y/z URL path and Range requests.

If all you want is the world map, getting it is as simple as going to the build page and downloading the latest daily build.

However, more fun can be had with the CLI . For example, you can extract data for only a bounding box or specific zoom levels, to get a significantly smaller file.

One great CDN for deploying this is Bunny.net (affiliate link) . They support HTTP Range requests, don’t collect personal data by default, 2 are headquartered in the EU, and offer low-cost access to a global network of CDN and edge storage servers.

Pricing varies based on region and replication factor of the edge storage. But generally you pay $0.01/GB ($0.005/GB on the smaller Volume network) for bandwidth to Europe and North America, and $0.01/GB/month (no replication) to $0.055/GB/month (maximum replication) for storage. A high degree of replication mostly matters for latency in case of a cache miss (as the data is further replicated when it’s cached at the CDN PoPs).

In practical terms, storing the 139GB world map with replication to most continents (5x) will run you about $5/month in storage fees. Loading a map of Europe on a laptop and zooming in on a city causes about 5MB of data to be transmitted, which would be $0.00005 — further navigations and reloads will be less expensive as more of the map gets cached locally. At $0.05/1k map loads that could be 100x cheaper than Mapbox. However, the actual bandwidth of course varies (less for people that bounce immediately, possibly tens of MB for heavy users). For Mapbox you only pay a flat fee per visit.

It’s a good idea to create a storage zone with S3 compatibility enabled, as uploading via the HTTP API timed out after 15 minutes for me.

Then, with rclone installed, you can download and stream the file to the Bunny storage zone. Preferably in tmux or from a temporary VPS, if your connection isn’t great.

endpoint="https://<primary-region>-s3.storage.bunnycdn.com"

rclone copyurl "<build-url>" "bunnycdn:<zone-name>/<filename>.pmtiles" \

Theoretically, at this point you just need to create a pull zone, select the storage zone as an origin, and you’re done. Practically, it would be sensible to change some settings.

Allowed CORS origins can be configured under Security > General > Allowed referrers, so that other websites cannot embed your tiles.

You’ll also want to verify under Caching that “Optimize for large object delivery” is enabled, as this makes it possible to cache Range requests.

You might also want to dissuade people from downloading the whole file and leaving you with a large CDN bill. The most practical way I’ve found for this is limiting the download speed to 10kB/s after 10MB transmitted in a single request (using the “Download speed limits” and “Limit after” settings under “Network limits”). Regular usage should never reach this amount. You may further want to introduce a requests/second limit (do note that legitimate usage can also quickly reach high numbers here) or a monthly bandwidth limit for the pull zone.

With the tiles deployed, the only thing left to do is to embed them in your website via MapLibre…

items.title: Paint in the memory of other programs
items.content:
core is a program that I wrote which spills the viscera of other programs onto the screen and allows you to prod them. it could be called an “esoteric debugger” or a “paint program.”

the visual content of the program is constructed as follows:

as well as the display of program memory, core allows for its manipulation. if core shows you a picture of a program’s insides, then it is only natural that it allows you to scribble on it. the overcommitted empty space below the stack stack provides an inviting empty space to scribble in. it’s a perfect place to hide your terrible secrets in some poor, innocent process.

core is the logical conclusion of blinkenlights, “Allblinkenlights,” if you will. the intended experience is evocative aimlessness. the human visual system is highly parallel and very good at recognizing patterns. you are encouraged to allow these patterns to wash over you.

many textures arise from different kinds of data in memory. ASCII text is incredibly recognizable, by virtue of being a 7-bit encoding, as well as having a biased distribution of values. 64-bit pointers are similarly easy to recognize because their last two bytes will either be zero or one.

in the mesmerizing undulations of complex programs, these textures may blink or move around or stay boringly still. if you are keen, you may catch some large data structure being allocated or filled in. or you may see the first generation of a garbage collector fly by as short-lived objects are created at a rapid rate. in games, the stack can be seen flickering rapidly and changing every frame.

core can make stark the immensity of memory and the way that programs use it. data structures and programming patterns appear in the physical reality of which bits are toggled where.

I was very keen to see what a program would look like that uses continuation passing style implemented as in the famous paper, CONS should not CONS its arguments, part II: Cheney on the M.T.A . I compiled a game programmed in CHICKEN scheme and was delighted to see a stack that moved like a waterfall.

graphical programs can be the most interesting. visual patterns in graphics in memory can emerge vividly.

when attached to virtual machines or emulators, core gains omniscience over an entire operating system.

it is astounding to see an immense creature flicker to life. pages fill empty space in speckled patterns. panning over a chasm, the page tables can be seen vibrating and filling in with new allocations. it is reminiscent, perhaps, of insects, like a beehive.

one could not hope to wholly understand the way that physical memory is arranged, but they may peer voyeuristically into random pages of process memory, abound with text strings and recognizable graphics.

programs often exist in the mind as something ineffable, intangible, and abstract. even their physical existence is locked inside black plastic squares, harboring impossibly tiny transistors. in my opinion, to lay visceral the individual bits in a computer program is an idea that despite being simple, is immensely potent.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Accessibility and the EU AI Act
items.content:
The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) is already in force, with more of its rules coming into effect each year until 2028. So what does it mean if you build AI or use third-party AI tools, and where does accessibility fit in?

The Act is a framework for ensuring AI is safe and respects people’s fundamental rights. It promotes better governance of AI, and transparency when it’s used. If you’re building or using artificial intelligence in your consumer products in the EU, then you are subject to the Act.

The AI Act makes compliance with the Web Accessibility Directive and the European Accessibility Act (EAA) a legal requirement for providers of high-risk AI from December 2027. In practice, this means products and services meeting EN 301 549 and the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 .

The Act also requires that people are told when they’re interacting with AI or AI-generated content, and that this information is accessible. This applies to more than high-risk AI.

If you provide or deploy an AI tool in the EU, you’re subject to the Act, including if you’re based outside the EU but your customers are in the EU.

A provider is an organisation that develops and markets AI systems. This can be anything from chatbots and virtual assistants to screening tools and AI image generators.

A deployer is an organisation that integrates these third-party AI tools. This could be a financial institution using AI to predict monthly spending or a retailer using an AI chatbot to answer customer queries.

The Act sets out duties that companies providing or deploying AI must meet categorised into four risk levels: unacceptable, high, limited, or minimal risk.

Each risk level has different duties. However, there is a common requirement at each level: organisations must take steps to help staff build AI literacy so they understand AI well enough to use it safely.

This is AI that threatens people’s safety or rights, for example social scoring, emotion recognition in the workplace, or AI that exploits people’s age, disability , or circumstances. From December 2026, it also includes AI that generates non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

The requirement here is clear-cut. The Act states that this type of AI must not be used.

This is AI that makes or supports significant decisions about people, for example recruitment screening, university admissions, credit scoring, and benefit eligibility.

Most of the Act’s duties sit here. If you build high-risk AI, you must manage its risks, make sure people can oversee it, prove it complies, and make it accessible . If you deploy high-risk AI, you must use it as intended, monitor it, and tell people when it’s used.

This is AI that interacts with people or creates content, for example chatbots, virtual assistants, image generators, and writing tools.

You must tell people when they’re interacting with AI, and label AI-generated content as AI. The labels must also be accessible.

This covers AI that poses little or no risk to people. This includes spam filters, AI in video games, route planning, and product recommendations.

There are no specific duties under the Act, but voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.

If you are using AI, here are some steps you can take to get ready for the Act:

The Act doesn't replace accessibility law, it reinforces it. Whatever your sector, if you build or use AI, accessibility needs to be part of how you choose, build, and govern it.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-99307 📢 Source: Linux 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ceph: require the dentry lease record to cover struct ceph_mds_reply_lease parse_reply_info_lease() reads a 32-bit struct_len off the wire and only checks that many bytes are present, without requiring struct_len to cover sizeof(struct ceph_mds_reply_lease) (10 bytes). A malicious MDS can declare a shorter record and still get the pointer published: the following *p += sizeof(**lease) overshoot is undone by *p = lend, so nothing downstream rejects the reply. ceph_fill_trace() -> update_dentry_lease() then reads 10 bytes through that pointer on any lookup on a mounted CephFS, running past the end of the message front. Require the record to cover the structure, matching the sibling parse_reply_info_dir(). A conforming MDS always encodes the full 10 bytes. BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in __update_dentry_lease.constprop.0 (fs/ceph/inode.c:1459) Read of size 4 at addr ffff888026c63d65 by task kworker/0:3/2366 Workqueue: ceph-msgr ceph_con_workfn Call Trace: __update_dentry_lease.constprop.0 (fs/ceph/inode.c:1459) ceph_fill_trace (fs/ceph/inode.c:1474 fs/ceph/inode.c:1823) mds_dispatch (fs/ceph/mds_client.c:4229 fs/ceph/mds_client.c:7225) ceph_con_process_message (net/ceph/messenger.c:1424) ceph_con_v1_try_read (net/ceph/messenger_v1.c:1430) ceph_con_workfn (net/ceph/messenger.c:1576) process_one_work (kernel/workqueue.c:3396) worker_thread (kernel/workqueue.c:3479 kernel/workqueue.c:3560) kthread (kernel/kthread.c:436) ret_from_fork (arch/x86/kernel/process.c:158) ret_from_fork_asm (arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S:245) The buggy address is located 357 bytes inside of allocated 360-byte region [ffff888026c63c00, ffff888026c63d68) 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-16T09:59:31.234Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-99307
items.title_ko: CVE-2026-99307: Linux 커널 ceph 덴트리 리스 레코드 길이 검증 누락
items.summary_ko: Linux 커널 ceph의 parse_reply_info_lease()가 레코드 길이를 구조체 크기(10바이트)만큼 요구하지 않아, 악의적인 MDS가 짧은 레코드를 보내면 CephFS에서 조회 시 메시지 범위를 벗어나는 KASAN slab-out-of-bounds 읽기가 발생할 수 있다. 수정안은 레코드가 구조체 전체를 포함하도록 검사하는 것이다. 원문 메타데이터상 CVSS 점수는 0.0 (NA), 원격 악용 가능 여부는 False로 표기돼 있다.
items.content_ko: 커널 ceph 파서는 MDS 응답의 struct_len을 32비트로 읽고, 그 길이만큼 바이트가 존재하는지만 확인한다. struct_len이 ceph_mds_reply_lease 구조체(10바이트)를 포함하는지는 검사하지 않는다. 악의적인 MDS는 짧은 레코드를 선언하면서도 포인터를 전달받을 수 있고, 뒤따르는 *p += sizeof(**lease)의 오버슛은 *p = lend로 되돌려져 하위 로직에서 거부되지 않는다. 그 결과 CephFS 마운트 상태에서 조회가 일어나면 update_dentry_lease 경로가 메시지 끝을 넘어 10바이트를 읽는다. 수정안은 형제 함수인 parse_reply_info_dir()과 같이 레코드가 구조체를 완전히 포함하도록 요구하는 것이다. 정상적인 MDS는 항상 10바이트 전체를 인코딩한다. 원문에는 fs/ceph/inode.c:1459에서 발생한 4바이트 읽기의 KASAN 로그가 포함돼 있다.

items.title: beer.drv.drv.drv
items.content:
Have you heard about dynamic derivations ?

They are an experimental-feature in Nix that lets a derivation produce other derivations as its output. Why ? This lets you dynamically create your build graph, instead of having to know it all at evaluation time. It’s Nix’s answer to try and match the build speed of other build systems like Bazel or buck2 .

There is not much written about dynamic derivations, and the documentation is sparse. I have written a few posts about them, so I sometimes get questions about them.

Recently, I got a DM from Evan Porter over LinkedIn , the ultimate bug triaging network, about whether it is possible to query the deriver of a dynamic derivation to get the initial derivation.

For dynamic derivations let’s say I have a .drv.drv file. This file outputs a derivation.

Is it usually possible to query deriver the output derivation to obtain the initial derivation?

$ ( nix-store --query --deriver ./result )

That should work. 🤨 Every path a build registers carries a deriver , the .drv that produced it, and a .drv that came out of a build is still a path a build registered.

You will need extra-experimental-features = dynamic-derivations ca-derivations recursive-nix in your nix.conf to drive the samples in this post.

/nix/store/v4hkwn8y4m083gsap6523c0m5r985ygr-result

/nix/store/v4hkwn8y4m083gsap6523c0m5r985ygr-result

/nix/store/6pniymfhwcyrmkns0np7ap1argjziqq2-result.drv

/nix/store/6pniymfhwcyrmkns0np7ap1argjziqq2-result.drv

/nix/store/m5x261fv29jkn0rvznqj2fzkaql01xiy-result.drv.drv

Turns out, there is a case where you do get unknown-deriver if you set __contentAddressed = true on the producer. If the producer is content-addressed, its output path is not known until after the build, and Nix does not fill in the deriver of a path that already exists.

The question though made me wonder how far back you can walk the chain of dynamic derivations. I had to try it. 😈

Let’s pick a fun example to see how far we can go. Here is a derivation that imitates the classic song 99 bottles of beer by producing a chain of derivations, each one outputting the next verse. 1 1 The builder writes the next derivation by hand in ATerm , so there is no recursive Nix and no nix-instantiate involved.

# A content-addressed derivation does not know its output path, so its

# "out" variable holds this placeholder and Nix swaps in the real path at

# build time. It is "/" + nix32(sha256("nix-output:out")), the same for

# every derivation with an output named "out".

OUT_PLACEHOLDER = /1rz4g4znpzjwh1xymhjpm42vipw92pr73vdgl6xs1hycac8kf2n9

# The last derivation in the chain writes the punchline instead of a .drv.

echo "No more bottles of beer on the wall, no more bottles of beer." > &2

echo "Go to the store and buy some more." > $out

echo " $( bottles $n ) of beer on the wall, $( bottles $n ) of beer." > &2

echo "Take one down, pass it around, $( bottles $next ) of beer on the wall." > &2

srcs = $( printf '"%s"\n' " $busybox " " $script " | sort | paste -sd , - )

# Write the derivation for the next verse. A .drv is a single line of

# ATerm, so strip the spaces and newlines that are only here for reading.

# Nix takes a derivation's name from its store path, so the next name is

A derivation whose output is a .drv must set outputHashMode = "text" .

In our example we are using a content-addressed derivation, but the same idea works with an input-addressed one, but it’s more work to compute the output path in the shell, unless you are using nix-instantiate to do it for you with recursive Nix.

The Nix side builds the first derivation and then follows builtins.outputOf once per bottle.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…
